newsitem.title: USA: Reno says she won't give in to pressure on counsel.
newsitem.headline: Reno says she won't give in to pressure on counsel.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno said Wednesday she would not be pressured by Congress to seek an independent counsel to investigate campaign fund-raising activities by the Clinton administration.

"If at any time I find that the requirements of the independent counsel act have been met, I will not hesitate to invoke it -- as I have in the past," Reno said at a day-long Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.

"But let me be absolutely clear. I am not going to violate any oath in this matter because of any pressure from any quarter, not from the media, not from Congress, not from anywhere else. And I'm not going to do things based on polls."

Reno was responding to criticism from committee chairman Orrin Hatch of Utah and other Republicans about her refusal to seek an independent counsel to investigate allegations that President Clinton's re-election campaign accepted illegal contributions from foreigners.

"If ever there was a case where public confidence in the integrity of an investigation, and in the Justice Department itself, required a prosecutor who is not a political appointee of the president, it is here," Hatch told Reno.

The department is conducting its own investigation of the fund-raising but Hatch said the law required an independent counsel because allegations that Clinton, Vice President Al Gore and other administration officials were involved created at least an appearance of conflict of interest.

But Reno said the law required an actual conflict of interest before an independent counsel was appointed. She said there was no clear and convincing evidence that any officials covered by the independent counsel law were involved.
Hatch said he disagreed with Reno's interpretation of the law but did not question her integrity. "I believe you are an honest person," he told her.

"I've got to go with the facts. I may be wrong," Reno said. She promised to review Hatch's arguments and consider any new evidence, but added, "We need specific and credible evidence, not suspicions."
Alabama Republican Jeff Sessions suggested Reno's decision might be questioned because she could be replaced by Clinton. "If I do what I think is right and I don't have a job, too bad," Reno replied.

Most of the committee Democrats defended Reno. "I believe Attorney General Janet Reno has more credibility on this issue than the many Republicans in Congress who are trying to compel her into doing something she clearly feels is unjustified by the law," Sen. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts said.
"I am confident that she's going to do what she thinks is right," added Vermont Democrat Patrick Leahy.
"This (hearing) ... is an effort to pressure you. I think you're doing the right thing," Dick Durbin of Illinois said.

But Wisconsin Democrat Russ Feingold said he believed an independent counsel should be appointed. "I believe the weight of the evidence supports the conclusion that such a request is not only appropriate but necessary," he said.

The fund-raising investigation has involved possible attempts at illegal or improper influence-peddling by foreign donors, mainly from Asia, as well as U.S. sources in financing the campaign that re-elected Clinton last year.
Reno has sought the appointment of four independent counsels in the four years she has been in office including one to investigate Clinton's involvement in the Whitewater land deal in Arkansas.
